lines.text: אבל 8 אבן
and long grass, sea-weed. So 1 Sam.
6, 18, unless instead of אָבֵל הַגְּדֹלָה it
should read אֶבֶן הָגְּדֹלָה which the con-
text in v. 14. 15, seems to demand, and
which is expressed by Sept. and Syr.—It
is frequent in geographical pr. names:
a) אָבֵל בֵּית־מַעֲכָה Abel Beth-Maachah
i. e. situated near Beth-Maachah q. v.
[now called Abil el-Kamh, a town on the
west side of the valley leading from
Merj 'Ayûn to the plain of the Hûleh,
west of Paneas and Dan; see Biblioth.
where אָבֵל־מַיִם Abel-maim 2 Chr. 16, 4,
comp. 1 K. 15, 20. Also simpl. אָבֵל
b) אָבֵל הַשִּׁטִּים Abel-shittim (acacia-
meadow) Num. 33, 49; a place in the
plains of Moab, prob. the same which in
Num. 25, 1. Mic. 6, 5, is called simpl.
שִׁטִּים.
c) אָבֵל כְּרָמִים Abel-keramim, (mea-
dow of vineyards) Judg. 11, 33; a village
of the Ammonites, according to Euse-
bius still rich in vineyards in his day.
d) אָבֵל מְחוֹלָה (meadow of dancing)
Abel-meholah, a village of Issachar, not
far from Scythopolis, the birth-place of
the prophet Elisha, Judg. 7, 22. 1 K. 4,
e) אָבֵל מִצְרַיִם Gen. 50, 11 (meadow
of the Egyptians) Abel-Mizraim, name
of an area or threshing-floor near the
Jordan. Here prob. we should read
with other points, and pronounce אֵבֶל
מִצְרַיִם, i. e. mourning of the Egyptians;
see the context.
אֵבֶל m. (r. אָבַל I,) c. suff. אֶבְלִי,
mourning, lamentation, Esth. 4, 3. 9, 22;
espec. for the dead, Gen. 27, 41. אֵבֶל
יָחִיד mourning for an only son, Am. 8,
10. Jer. 6, 26. Mic. 1, 8 וְאֵבֶל כִּבְנוֹת יַעֲנָה
a mourning as of ostriches, which make
a wailing cry. עָשָׂה אֵבֶל לְ to make a
mourning for any one, Gen. 50, 10.
אֲבָל adv. 1) Affirmative, in the earlier
Hebrew, truly, certainly, indeed, Gen.
with a corrective sense, nay indeed, nay
rather, immo vero, Gen. 17, 19. 1 K. 1, 43.—
It corresponds to the Arabic corrective
partic. بَلْ but indeed, but more, nay
rather; and is derived from r. בְּלָה, pr.
i. q. Heb. בַּל, so that its primary force
seems to lie in denying the contrary.
The א is prosthetic.
2. In later writers, adversative, but,
but yet, nevertheless, Dan. 10, 7. 21.
but.—Other particles of this kind, which
are both affirmative and adversative, are
אַךְ, אָכֵן. Comp. Lat. verum, vero.
אֻבָל see אוּבָל.
* אָבַן obsol. root, prob. to build,
comp. בָּנָה to build, and אָמַן to prop, to
support, to found, whence אָמָן artisan,
τέκτων. Hence
אֶבֶן, in pause אָבֶן, c. suff. אַבְנוֹ; plur.
אֲבָנִים, constr. אַבְנֵי; comm. gend. most-
ly fem. and so even Job 28, 2; but m.
1. a stone, of any kind, whether rough
or polished, large or small. Collect.
stones, Gen. 11, 3. Spoken of a founda-
tion stone, Is. 28, 16; of vessels of stone
Ex. 7, 19. Syr. ܐܰܓܡܳܐ id. but rare. Eth.
እብን.—Metaph. 1 Sam. 25, 37 and he
became stone, i. e. stiff, rigid like stone.
לֵב הָאֶבֶן the heart of stone, i. e. hard, ob-
durate, Ez. 11, 19. 36, 26; also of firm
undaunted courage Job 41, 16. אֶבֶן בָּרָד
collect. hailstones Is. 30, 30; whence
Josh. 10, 11 אֲבָנִים גְּדֹלוֹת large hail-
stones, called just afterwards אַבְנֵי הַבָּרָד.
2. Spec. a precious stone, gem, Ex.
28, 9 sq. 35, 27; more fully אֶבֶן חֵפֶץ
Is. 54, 12; אֶבֶן חֵן Prov. 17, 8; אֶבֶן
יְקָרָה Ez. 28, 13; which last is also said
of finer kinds of stones for building, as
3. stone-ore, ore, Job 28, 2. Comp.
Arabic dual حَجَرَتَانِ the two stones,
ores, i. e. gold and silver.
4. a rock, Gen. 49, 24 אֶבֶן יִשְׂרָאֵל the
rock of Israel, i. e. Jehovah; comp. צוּר.
5. a weight of a balance, even when
not made of stone; since anciently, as
at the present day, the Orientals often
made use of stones for weights; comp.
Engl. stone for a weight of 14 pounds,
Germ. Stein. אֶבֶן וָאֶבֶן diverse weights,
Deut. 25, 13. אַבְנֵי כִיס weights of the
bag, i. e. carried about in a bag, Prov.

line_status.note: The final letter of the right-hand word is a narrow descending stroke with a small head (final nun ן), not the wide-topped final kaf ך; alphabetically a running head אבל…אבן is also the only possible order, since אבך would precede אבל.

Under the ה of הגדלה the printed vowel has a bar with a downward tick (qamets), unlike the flat patach printed on the same word in line 2 above; so Reading B's הָ is what is printed, even though הַ would be the grammatically expected form.

Under the bet the print shows two vertically stacked dots (shewa, בְּ), not a single qamets stroke; lamed carries qamets, he is unpointed. Reading A's בָּלָה is wrong. (A thin typographic space precedes the semicolon, as usual in this edition.)
Under the first aleph the print shows three dots in a descending diagonal (qibbuts), not shewa+patah; אֻבָל is the defective form of אוּבָל, which fits the cross-reference. Reading A is correct.

The Syriac consonants are ܐܓܡܐ (gamal–mim, cognate of אֲגַם), as in B, not ܒܢ as in A; but the vowel over the first alaph is the alpha-shaped pthaha (ܰ), as A has it, not rbasa (ܶ); the omicron-shaped zqapha (ܳ) over mim is agreed. So the correct form is ܐܰܓܡܳܐ.
